meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.concept: Interpreting a multiple regression coefficient (Section 13.1, Key Concept 13.1)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of county average test scores on median household income (in $1,000s), the percent of adults with a college degree, and average class size gives a coefficient of 1.8 on income. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Raising a county's median income by $1,000 would raise its test scores by exactly 1.8 points.
options.feedback: Not quite. Observational data give an association, and the coefficient holds the other regressors fixed; it is not a guaranteed causal effect.

options.text: Across all counties, $1,000 more median income goes with test scores 1.8 points higher, without holding anything else fixed.
options.feedback: Not quite. That describes a bivariate slope. In a multiple regression, each coefficient holds the other regressors constant.

options.text: Comparing counties with the same college share and class size, $1,000 more median income is associated with test scores about 1.8 points higher.
options.feedback: Correct. A multiple regression coefficient is a partial effect: it compares units that are alike on the other regressors.

options.text: Median income explains about 1.8% of the variation in test scores across counties.
options.feedback: Not quite. Shares of variation explained come from R², not from a slope coefficient.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.1: each coefficient in a multiple regression is a partial association, holding the other regressors constant. With observational data it is not automatically causal.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of county test scores on the college-degree share alone gives a slope of 2.4, while a multiple regression that adds income and class size gives a college-share coefficient of 1.6. Counties A and B have the same income and class size, but A's college share is 5 percentage points higher. By about how much does the multiple regression predict A's score to exceed B's?

options.text: About 8 points
options.feedback: Correct: 5 × 1.6 = 8 points. The counties match on the other regressors, so the partial coefficient applies.

options.text: About 12 points
options.feedback: Not quite. 5 × 2.4 = 12 uses the bivariate slope, which also picks up differences in income and class size that these counties do not have.

options.text: About 1.6 points
options.feedback: Not quite. 1.6 is the change for a 1-point difference; multiply by the 5-point gap.

options.text: About 0.32 points
options.feedback: Not quite. 1.6 ÷ 5 divides by the gap instead of multiplying by it.

practice.explanation: Section 13.1: with the other regressors equal, the predicted gap is coefficient × difference = 1.6 × 5 = 8 points.

practice.concept: Interpreting a coefficient in a house-price regression (Section 13.1)
practice.stem: Suppose that across 300 houses the correlation between price and the number of bedrooms is +0.40 and bedrooms and size have a correlation of 0.70, but in a regression of price on size (square feet) and bedrooms, the bedrooms coefficient is −2,000 with p ≈ 0.60. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The negative coefficient shows that houses with more bedrooms sell for less, on average.
options.feedback: Not quite. On average, houses with more bedrooms sell for more (r = +0.40). The coefficient compares houses of the same size, and it is not significant.

options.text: Holding size fixed, the data show little evidence that extra bedrooms are associated with price.
options.feedback: Correct. With p ≈ 0.60, the partial effect of bedrooms cannot be distinguished from zero.

options.text: Adding bedrooms to a regression that already contains size must lower R².
options.feedback: Not quite. Adding a regressor never lowers R² in OLS; it can only stay the same or rise.

options.text: Bedrooms is correlated with size, so its simple correlation with price partly reflects size.
options.feedback: Correct. Bigger houses tend to have more bedrooms, so the simple correlation mixes the two.

options.text: Bedrooms should be dropped from the regression because its coefficient has the 'wrong' sign.
options.feedback: Not quite. An unexpected or insignificant sign is not by itself a reason to drop a variable; report the specification and interpret it.

practice.explanation: Section 13.1: a simple correlation and a partial coefficient answer different questions. Once size is held fixed, bedrooms adds little; its positive simple correlation largely reflects its link with size.

practice.stem: Suppose that at every school the percent of fully credentialed teachers and the percent of teachers without full credentials sum to exactly 100. OLS can still estimate separate coefficients for both variables in a regression that includes an intercept.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Not quite. When one regressor is an exact linear function of another plus the intercept, OLS cannot separate their coefficients.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The two percentages are perfectly collinear with the intercept (one equals 100 minus the other), so OLS cannot estimate both; one must be dropped.

practice.explanation: Section 13.1: correlated regressors make coefficients imprecise; perfectly collinear ones make them impossible to estimate separately.

practice.concept: Estimating a nonlinear model by OLS (Section 13.2, Key Concept 13.2)
practice.stem: Suppose a demand model is Q = A·P<sup>β₂</sup>·I<sup>β₃</sup>, where Q is quantity, P is price, and I is income. Why would a researcher take natural logs of Q, P, and I before using OLS?

options.text: Logs remove the correlation of the errors across consecutive time periods.
options.feedback: Not quite. Taking logs changes the functional form; it does not address correlation of the errors over time.

options.text: Logs make price and income uncorrelated with each other, so their effects can be separated.
options.feedback: Not quite. Logs change the scale of the variables, not whether they move together.

options.text: OLS can be used only when every variable is measured as a percentage.
options.feedback: Not quite. OLS works with variables in any units; the issue is the form of the model.

options.text: In logs the model becomes ln Q = ln A + β₂ ln P + β₃ ln I, an equation OLS can fit directly.
options.feedback: Correct. The log equation has the same form as any OLS regression, so ln A, β₂, and β₃ can be estimated.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.2: after taking logs, ln Q = ln A + β₂ ln P + β₃ ln I is an ordinary regression equation whose slopes are elasticities.

practice.stem: Suppose an estimated production function is ln Q = 0.50 + 0.35 ln K + 0.60 ln L. Holding labor fixed, by about how much does predicted output change if capital rises by 10%?

options.text: About 0.35%
options.feedback: Not quite. 0.35 is the change for a 1% rise; a 10% rise gives about 10 times as much.

options.text: About 3.5%
About 9.5%
options.feedback: Not quite. 9.5% adds both elasticities, which applies only when both inputs rise by 10%.

options.text: About 6.0%
options.feedback: Not quite. 0.60 is the labor elasticity; the question changes capital.

practice.explanation: Section 13.2: in a log-log model, a 1% change in an input changes output by about the coefficient in percent. Here 10% × 0.35 ≈ 3.5%.

practice.concept: Testing returns to scale (Section 13.2, Key Concept 13.3)
practice.stem: Suppose a Cobb-Douglas regression for an industry gives capital and labor elasticities that sum to 0.82, and the test of H₀: β₂ + β₃ = 1 gives p = 0.01. What is the best conclusion at the 5% level?

options.text: The data are consistent with constant returns to scale: H₀ is not rejected.
options.feedback: Not quite. p = 0.01 < 0.05, so H₀ is rejected.

options.text: Constant returns are rejected, and the estimates point to decreasing returns to scale.
options.feedback: Correct. p < 0.05 rejects H₀, and a sum below 1 means doubling both inputs less than doubles output.

options.text: Increasing returns are established, because the test rejects constant returns.
options.feedback: Not quite. Rejection says the sum differs from 1; here the sum is below 1, which points to decreasing returns.

options.text: The test is uninformative because the estimated sum is below 1.
options.feedback: Not quite. The test is designed exactly to judge whether a sum below (or above) 1 could be due to chance.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.3: the test of β₂ + β₃ = 1 checks constant returns. With p = 0.01 and a sum of 0.82, constant returns are rejected in favor of decreasing returns.

practice.stem: Suppose a Cobb-Douglas production function has β₂ + β₃ = 0.9. Then doubling both capital and labor raises output by less than double.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. With β₂ + β₃ = 0.9, doubling both inputs multiplies output by 2<sup>0.9</sup> ≈ 1.87: decreasing returns to scale.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Not quite. Scaling both inputs by 2 multiplies output by 2<sup>β₂+β₃</sup> = 2<sup>0.9</sup> ≈ 1.87, which is less than 2.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts: returns to scale are decreasing, constant, or increasing as β₂ + β₃ is below, equal to, or above 1.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of ln(wage) has a standard error of the regression \( s = 0.50 \). The retransformation correction multiplies \( e^{\widehat{\ln w}} \) by \( e^{s^2/2} \). What is the correction factor, approximately?

options.feedback: Not quite. \( e^{0.5} \approx 1.65 \) uses s instead of s²/2.
Not quite. \( e^{0.25} \approx 1.28 \) uses s² without dividing by 2.
Not quite. \( e^{0.0625} \approx 1.06 \) divides s² by 4 instead of 2.

practice.explanation: Section 13.2: the correction factor is \( e^{s^2/2} \); with \( s = 0.50 \) it is \( e^{0.125} \approx 1.13 \), so level predictions are raised by about 13%.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of annual wage growth (%) on the unemployment rate (%) for 1960–1985 has a slope of −0.80. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Years with 1 point more unemployment saw wage growth roughly 0.80 points lower, on average.
options.feedback: Correct. The slope compares years that differ by 1 point in the unemployment rate.

options.text: A year with wage growth 1 percentage point higher had unemployment about 0.80 points lower, on average.
options.feedback: Not quite. This reverses the roles: wage growth is the outcome, unemployment the regressor.

options.text: Raising unemployment by 1 percentage point would cause wage growth to fall by exactly 0.80 points.
options.feedback: Not quite. A time-series regression gives an association, not a guaranteed causal effect.

options.text: Wage growth averaged −0.80% per year over 1960–1985.
options.feedback: Not quite. The slope is not the average of the outcome.

practice.explanation: Section 13.3: a slope compares observations that differ by one unit of the regressor: here, years with 1 point more unemployment had 0.80 points less wage growth.

practice.concept: The Phillips curve breakdown (Section 13.3, Key Concept 13.4)
practice.stem: Stagflation refers to a period in which high unemployment and high inflation occur at the same time.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The 1970s combined high unemployment with high inflation, which the simple Phillips curve said should not happen together.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Not quite. Stagflation is exactly that combination: stagnation (high unemployment) with inflation.

practice.explanation: Section 13.3: stagflation in the 1970s contradicted the simple Phillips curve trade-off and motivated the expectations-augmented model.

practice.concept: The omitted variables bias formula (Section 13.3, Key Concept 13.5)
practice.stem: Suppose the true wage model is ln(wage) = β₁ + 0.08 × education + 0.05 × ability + u, and a regression of ability on education has slope γ = 0.60. Using E[b₂] = β₂ + β₃γ, what slope would a regression of ln(wage) on education alone be expected to give?

options.feedback: Not quite. 0.05 × 0.60 = 0.03 is the bias alone; add it to the true coefficient.
Not quite. 0.08 − 0.03 subtracts the bias; here β₃γ is positive and is added.
Not quite. 0.08 + 0.05 adds β₃ without multiplying by γ.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.5: E[b₂] = β₂ + β₃γ = 0.08 + 0.05 × 0.60 = 0.11, so omitting ability overstates the return to education.

practice.stem: In the same wage example (β₂ = 0.08 on education, β₃ = 0.05 on ability, γ = 0.60), which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Omitting ability makes the education coefficient too large in this example.
options.feedback: Correct. The bias β₃γ is positive, so the short regression overstates β₂.

options.text: The bias arises because ability affects wages and is also correlated with education.
options.feedback: Correct. Both ingredients of β₃γ are nonzero.

options.text: Adding a good measure of ability as a regressor would reduce the bias.
options.feedback: Correct. Controlling for the omitted variable removes the channel through which it biases b₂.

options.text: The bias would vanish if both regressions used heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors instead of default ones.
options.feedback: Not quite. Robust standard errors change inference, not the coefficient, so they cannot remove bias.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.5: omitted variables bias = β₃γ. It needs the omitted variable to matter for y and to be correlated with the included regressor; changing the standard errors does not touch it.

practice.stem: Suppose a log-log regression of house prices on size gives an elasticity of 0.70, controlling for location and age. Holding the other regressors fixed, how does the price of a house that is 20% larger differ?

options.text: About 0.14% higher
options.feedback: Not quite. The coefficient is a percent-for-percent elasticity: 20% × 0.70 ≈ 14%.

options.text: About $14 higher
options.feedback: Not quite. In a log-log model the effect is in percent, not dollars.

options.text: About 14% higher
About 70% higher
options.feedback: Not quite. 0.70 is the elasticity, the percent change for a 1% change in size.

practice.explanation: Section 13.4: in a log-log model, the coefficient is an elasticity: a 20% larger house is about 0.70 × 20 ≈ 14% more expensive, other things fixed.

practice.concept: Time trends in a log model (Section 13.4)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of ln(laptop price) on processor speed, memory, screen size, and model year gives a year coefficient of −0.12. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Holding the specifications fixed, prices were about 12% lower for each later model year.
options.feedback: Correct. With a log outcome, a coefficient of −0.12 means about 12% lower per year, for laptops with the same specifications.

options.text: Average laptop prices fell by about 12% per year over the sample period.
options.feedback: Not quite. The coefficient holds specifications fixed; average prices also reflect changes in what laptops offer.

options.text: Holding the specifications fixed, prices fell by about $0.12 per year.
options.feedback: Not quite. With ln(price) as the outcome, the coefficient is a proportional change, not dollars.

options.text: Holding the specifications fixed, prices fell by about 0.12% per year.
options.feedback: Not quite. Multiply the coefficient by 100 to get the percent change: about 12%.

practice.explanation: Section 13.4: with a log outcome, 100 × coefficient ≈ percent change per year, holding the other regressors fixed (about −12% here).

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of test scores uses 5,000 students from 200 schools, with standard errors clustered by school. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Students in the same school share teachers and neighborhoods, so their errors may be correlated.
options.feedback: Correct. That shared environment is the reason to cluster by school.

options.text: Clustering by school changes the estimated coefficients.
options.feedback: Not quite. Clustering changes only the standard errors; the OLS coefficients are the same.

options.text: Clustering lets errors of students in the same school be correlated while treating different schools as independent.
options.feedback: Correct. That is exactly what cluster-robust standard errors allow.

options.text: With clustered standard errors, confidence intervals usually become wider.
options.feedback: Correct. Larger standard errors mean more conservative inference.

options.text: Clustering is unnecessary when the coefficients are significant with default standard errors.
options.feedback: Not quite. Default standard errors can be too small under clustering, so significance with them can be misleading.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.6: grouped data call for cluster-robust standard errors. They leave coefficients unchanged and are typically larger than default standard errors.

practice.stem: Suppose houses got larger over time while the construction cost per square foot of a house of a given size fell each year. Then the average construction cost per house must have fallen over time.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Not quite. Falling cost per square foot can be offset by building larger houses, so the average cost per house could stay flat or rise.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. A falling cost for a house of given size can be more than offset by the shift to larger houses.

practice.explanation: Section 13.4: an improvement for a product of given size can be offset by a shift toward larger products, so averages need not improve.

practice.concept: Observational comparisons of programs (Section 13.5, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: Suppose a school compares end-of-year exam scores of students who chose to attend an optional tutoring program with those of students who did not. Why might the difference not measure the effect of tutoring?

options.text: Because exam scores must be standardized before two groups can be compared
options.feedback: Not quite. Standardizing scores changes units, not who is in each group.

options.text: Because a regression of exam scores on a tutoring dummy always has a low R²
options.feedback: Not quite. R² measures fit; it says nothing about whether the groups are comparable.

options.text: Because students who choose tutoring may differ in motivation or prior achievement, which also affect scores
options.feedback: Correct. Self-selection mixes the program's effect with the traits of the students who choose it.

options.text: Because the comparison needs at least as many tutored as untutored students
options.feedback: Not quite. Unequal group sizes reduce precision, but they do not create bias.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts (Selection Bias): when units choose their treatment, traits that drive the choice can also drive the outcome. Random assignment is the standard fix.

practice.stem: Suppose a randomized job-training experiment regresses annual earnings on a training indicator. The intercept is $18,400 and the coefficient on training is $1,250. What is the predicted average earnings of the trained group?

options.feedback: Not quite. The coefficient is the difference from the control group, not the trained group's level.
Not quite. 18,400 − 1,250 subtracts a positive treatment effect.
Not quite. The intercept is the control group's mean.

practice.explanation: Section 13.5: with a single treatment dummy, the intercept is the control mean and the coefficient is the treatment–control difference, so the treated mean is 18,400 + 1,250 = $19,650.

practice.stem: In a randomized experiment, a low R² in the regression of the outcome on the treatment indicators means the estimated treatment effects are biased.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Not quite. R² measures how much of the outcome's variation the treatments explain; random assignment, not R², determines whether the estimates are unbiased.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Most variation in outcomes (for example, health shocks) is unrelated to treatment, so R² is low, yet randomization keeps the effect estimates unbiased.

practice.explanation: Section 13.5: R² measures how much of the outcome's variation the treatments explain. With random assignment, a low R² is compatible with unbiased treatment effects.

practice.stem: Suppose an experiment randomly assigns savers to a control group, a text-message reminder, or a letter reminder. Relative to control (mean savings $200), the text coefficient is +$40 (p = 0.01) and the letter coefficient is +$15 (p = 0.48); a joint F-test gives p = 0.03. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Both reminders significantly raise savings at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Not quite. The letter's p = 0.48 is far above 0.05.

options.text: The text group's predicted mean savings is $240.
The text reminder raises savings by about 40%.
options.feedback: Not quite. +$40 relative to a $200 control mean is a 20% increase.

options.text: Because assignment was random, comparing group means needs no control variables to give unbiased effects.
options.feedback: Correct. With random assignment, the treatment groups differ from control only by chance, so the simple comparison of means is unbiased.

practice.explanation: Section 13.5: with random assignment, each coefficient is an unbiased treatment–control difference in means. Dollar coefficients become percentages only after dividing by the control mean (40 / 200 = 20%).

practice.stem: Suppose average test scores in schools that adopted a new reading program rose from 50 to 58, while in schools that did not adopt it they rose from 47 to 51. What is the difference-in-differences estimate of the program's effect?

options.text: 4 points
8 points
options.feedback: Not quite. 8 is the before/after change in adopting schools, which includes the common trend.

options.text: 7 points
options.feedback: Not quite. 58 − 51 compares the groups only after adoption and ignores their initial gap.

options.text: 12 points
options.feedback: Not quite. 8 + 4 adds the two changes; DiD subtracts the control group's change.

practice.explanation: Section 13.6: DiD = (treated after − treated before) − (control after − control before) = 8 − 4 = 4 points.

practice.concept: The identifying assumption of DiD (Section 13.6, Key Concept 13.8)
practice.stem: Suppose a state's employment was already growing faster than its neighbor's before it raised its minimum wage. A DiD comparison of the two states' employment changes would still give an unbiased estimate of the law's effect.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Not quite. DiD uses the neighbor's change as the counterfactual; if the trends already differed, that counterfactual is wrong.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Faster pre-existing growth violates parallel trends, so the DiD estimate would mix the law's effect with the trend difference.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.8: DiD is unbiased only under parallel trends. Diverging pre-treatment trends are a warning sign.

practice.stem: In the regression y = β₁ + β₂ treat + β₃ post + β₄ (treat × post) + u, where treat = 1 for the treated group and post = 1 for the later period, what does β₁ measure?

options.text: The effect of the policy on the treated group
options.feedback: Not quite. The intercept is a group mean, not a difference.

options.text: The change over time in the control group's average outcome
options.feedback: Not quite. The intercept is a level, not a change.

options.text: The average outcome across all four group-period cells
options.feedback: Not quite. The intercept is the prediction for one specific cell.

options.text: The control group's average outcome in the earlier period
options.feedback: Correct. With treat = 0 and post = 0, the prediction is β₁.

practice.explanation: Section 13.6: setting treat = post = 0 gives y = β₁, the control group's mean before the policy; the other coefficients are differences from that baseline.

practice.stem: Suppose 40 schools adopted a new reading program in 2019 and 40 did not, with student test scores observed in 2017 and 2021. Which statements about a DiD analysis are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Scores from additional years before 2019 would help check whether the two groups of schools were trending in parallel.
options.feedback: Correct. Pre-program trends are the usual check on the parallel trends assumption.

options.text: The DiD estimate is credible only if the two groups of schools had the same average score in 2017, before the program began.
options.feedback: Not quite. DiD allows the groups to start at different levels; it requires parallel trends, not equal levels.

options.text: DiD removes the effect of any other policy adopted only by the program schools in 2020.
options.feedback: Not quite. A change that hits only the treated group between the periods is mixed into the DiD estimate.

options.text: If program schools' scores were already rising faster before 2019, the DiD estimate would overstate the program's effect.
options.feedback: Correct. A faster pre-existing trend would be credited to the program, biasing the estimate upward.

options.text: Comparing only the program schools' 2017 and 2021 scores would mix the program's effect with changes that affected all schools.
options.feedback: Correct. The control group's change is needed to remove common trends.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.8: DiD removes common time effects but relies on parallel trends; pre-program data help check it, and other treated-group-specific changes are not removed.

practice.concept: Interpreting a regression discontinuity estimate (Section 13.7, Key Concept 13.9)
practice.stem: Suppose students scoring below 50 on a placement test are assigned to a remedial math class. A regression of next-year math scores on a remedial indicator and the placement score gives a remedial coefficient of 3.0. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Every student assigned to remedial math gains exactly 3 points from it.
options.feedback: Not quite. RD estimates an average effect at the cutoff, and effects can differ across students.

options.text: Each extra point on the placement test raises next-year scores by 3 points.
options.feedback: Not quite. That would be the coefficient on the placement score, not on the remedial indicator.

options.text: Remedial students scored 3 points higher on the placement test than other students.
options.feedback: Not quite. The outcome is next-year math scores, not the placement score.

options.text: For students scoring near 50, remedial assignment raises next-year scores by about 3 points.
options.feedback: Correct. The jump at the cutoff estimates the effect for students close to it.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.9: the coefficient on the treatment indicator is the jump in the outcome at the cutoff, a local effect for units near it.

practice.stem: In the chapter's Senate data, win equals 1 exactly when margin is above zero, so treatment switches sharply at the threshold.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Treatment (winning, hence incumbency) is a deterministic function of the running variable: win = 1 if margin > 0.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Not quite. In the data, win = 1 for every election with a positive margin and 0 otherwise.

practice.explanation: Section 13.7: in a sharp RD design, treatment is fully determined by which side of the threshold the running variable falls on.

practice.stem: In the remedial-math example (assignment for scores below 50), which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Students scoring just above and just below 50 should be similar, apart from remedial assignment.
options.feedback: Correct. That near-equivalence is what makes the comparison at the cutoff credible.

options.text: Because assignment follows a rule, there is no need to focus on students near the cutoff.
options.feedback: Not quite. Far from the cutoff, students differ in ability, so the comparison loses its credibility.

options.text: If remedial classes matter, a plot of next-year scores against placement scores should show a jump at 50.
options.feedback: Correct. The effect appears as a discontinuity at the threshold.

options.text: The estimate applies equally to students who scored 10 or 90 on the placement test, since the same assignment rule covers them all.
options.feedback: Not quite. RD identifies the effect at the cutoff; it need not generalize far from it.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.9: RD compares units just on either side of a cutoff. The effect shows up as a jump and is local to the threshold.

practice.concept: Converting a log coefficient into a percentage (Section 13.8)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression gives ln(wage) = 2.1 + 0.40 × union, where union = 1 for union members. By about what percentage are union members' wages predicted to be higher?

options.text: About 149%
options.feedback: Not quite. 1.49 is the ratio of wages; the percentage increase is 49%.

options.text: About 49%
options.feedback: Correct: e<sup>0.40</sup> ≈ 1.49, so wages are about 49% higher.

options.text: About 33%
options.feedback: Not quite. 1 − e<sup>−0.40</sup> ≈ 0.33 is how much lower non-members' wages are relative to members'.

options.text: About 40%
options.feedback: Not quite. 100 × 0.40 is the log-point approximation, which is poor for a coefficient this large.

practice.explanation: Section 13.8: a coefficient b on a log outcome multiplies y by e<sup>b</sup>; e<sup>0.40</sup> ≈ 1.49, a 49% increase.

practice.concept: Conditions for a valid instrument (Section 13.8, Key Concept 13.10)
practice.stem: Suppose distance to the nearest college is used as an instrument for years of education in a wage regression. Critics note that people who live near colleges also tend to live in cities where wages are higher for everyone. Which instrument condition does this criticism challenge?

options.text: Relevance
options.feedback: Not quite. Relevance concerns the link between distance and education, which the criticism does not question.

options.text: Homoskedasticity
options.feedback: Not quite. The criticism is about a direct link to wages, not about error variance.

options.text: Exogeneity
options.feedback: Correct. If distance affects wages through local wage levels, the instrument is correlated with the error.

options.text: No perfect collinearity
options.feedback: Not quite. The criticism concerns a channel to wages, not an exact linear relationship among regressors.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 13.10: an instrument must be relevant (correlated with the endogenous regressor) and exogenous (unrelated to the error). A direct path from distance to wages breaks exogeneity.

practice.stem: Suppose the first-stage regression of an endogenous regressor on its instrument gives an F-statistic of 4. What should the researcher conclude?

options.text: The instrument is weak by the chapter's rule of thumb, so the 2SLS estimate may be unreliable.
options.feedback: Correct. The rule of thumb asks for F > 10; F = 4 signals a weak instrument.

options.text: The instrument is exogenous, because the first stage is statistically significant.
options.feedback: Not quite. The first stage speaks to relevance only; exogeneity cannot be checked this way.

options.text: The 2SLS estimate will be 4 times as large as the OLS estimate.
options.feedback: Not quite. The F-statistic does not scale the estimate.

options.text: The instrument explains 4% of the variation in the endogenous regressor.
options.feedback: Not quite. An F-statistic is not a share of variation explained.

practice.explanation: Section 13.8: a strong instrument needs a first-stage F above about 10; with F = 4, 2SLS can be badly biased and imprecise.

practice.stem: Suppose cities with more crime hire more police. In an OLS regression of the crime rate on police per capita across cities, how would this reverse causation bias the police coefficient?

options.text: Downward, making police look more effective at reducing crime than they are
options.feedback: Not quite. High-crime cities having more police pushes the coefficient up, not down.

options.text: Not at all, because police and crime are measured in the same cities
options.feedback: Not quite. Measuring both in the same cities is exactly what lets crime feed back into police.

options.text: Not at all, because police are measured per capita rather than as a count
options.feedback: Not quite. Measuring police per capita does not stop crime from feeding back into police hiring.

options.text: Upward, making police look less effective, or even crime-increasing
options.feedback: Correct. Crime raises police, creating a positive association that masks any crime-reducing effect.

practice.explanation: Section 13.8: reverse causation from y to x biases OLS in the direction of that feedback; here it pushes the coefficient upward. IV can address it.

practice.stem: Dataset 1 has ids 1, 2, and 3; dataset 2 has ids 1, 2, and 4. How many rows does an inner join on id produce?

options.text: 4 rows (ids 1, 2, 3, and 4)
options.feedback: Not quite. Keeping every id from both files is an outer join.

options.text: 3 rows (ids 1, 2, and 3)
options.feedback: Not quite. Keeping every id from the first file is a left join.

options.text: 3 rows (ids 1, 2, and 4)
options.feedback: Not quite. Keeping every id from the second file is a right join.

options.text: 2 rows (ids 1 and 2)
options.feedback: Correct. An inner join keeps only ids that appear in both files.

practice.explanation: Section 13.9: an inner join keeps only matching keys, so unmatched rows (ids 3 and 4) are dropped; always check how many observations a merge loses.

practice.stem: Suppose a researcher regresses profits on advertising for a cross-section of 500 firms of very different sizes and expects the error variance to grow with firm size. Which standard errors does the chapter recommend?

options.text: HAC (Newey–West) standard errors
options.feedback: Not quite. HAC standard errors target a different data structure than a single cross-section of firms.

options.text: Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors
options.feedback: Correct. HC1 standard errors handle error variance that differs across observations in a cross-section.

options.text: Standard errors clustered by firm
options.feedback: Not quite. With one observation per firm, each cluster would contain a single firm.

options.text: Default standard errors, since 500 firms is a large sample
options.feedback: Not quite. A large sample does not fix standard errors that assume constant error variance.

practice.explanation: Key Takeaways: for a cross-section with error variance that differs across observations, the chapter uses heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors.

practice.stem: Suppose a city has more applicants than places for a school voucher program and awards the vouchers by lottery. Researchers compare later outcomes of lottery winners and losers. Which method does this setting represent?

options.text: Randomized control trial
options.feedback: Correct. The lottery randomly assigns the vouchers among applicants.

options.text: Regression discontinuity
options.feedback: Not quite. There is no cutoff in a running variable; chance decides.

options.text: Instrumental variables
options.feedback: Not quite. Winners and losers are compared directly; no instrument for an endogenous regressor is needed.

options.text: Difference-in-differences
options.feedback: Not quite. The comparison does not rely on changes over time between groups.

practice.explanation: Sections 13.5–13.8: a lottery among applicants is random assignment, the RCT design.

exam.concept: Interpreting a multiple regression coefficient (Section 13.1, Key Concept 13.1)
exam.stem: In the chapter's regression of the 1999 Academic Performance Index (API) of 807 California high schools on edparent (average years of parent education), meals, englearn, yearround, credteach, and emerteach, the edparent coefficient is 73.9. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Each additional year of parent education raises a school's API by 73.9 points, whatever the school's other characteristics.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.1 and Key Concept 13.1 word a coefficient in a multiple regression.

options.text: Comparing schools with the same values of the other five regressors, one more year of parent education is associated with an API about 73.9 points higher.
options.feedback: Correct. It is a partial effect: an association that holds the other regressors constant.

options.text: Comparing all 807 schools, one more year of parent education is associated with an API about 73.9 points higher, without holding anything else fixed.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.1 and Key Concept 13.1 word a coefficient in a multiple regression.

options.text: Parent education alone explains about 73.9% of the variation in API across the 807 schools, once the other five regressors are included.
options.feedback: Revisit which regression output measures the share of variation explained (Section 13.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.1: 73.9 is the partial association of parent education with API, holding meals, English learners, year-round calendars, and the teacher-credential variables fixed. With observational data it is an association, not a causal effect.

exam.stem: For the 807 schools, regressing API on edparent alone gives a slope of 79.5; the multiple regression with the five other regressors gives an edparent coefficient of 73.9. Schools X and Y have the same meals, englearn, yearround, credteach, and emerteach, but average parent education is 1.5 years higher at X. By about how many points does the multiple regression predict X's API to exceed Y's?

options.text: About 74 points
options.feedback: Revisit how a predicted difference between two schools is computed from a regression (Section 13.1).

options.text: About 119 points
options.feedback: Revisit how a predicted difference between two schools is computed from a regression (Section 13.1).

options.text: About 49 points
options.feedback: Revisit how a predicted difference between two schools is computed from a regression (Section 13.1).

options.text: About 111 points
options.feedback: Correct: 1.5 × 73.9 ≈ 111 points. The schools match on the other regressors, so the multiple-regression coefficient applies.

exam.explanation: Section 13.1: with the other regressors equal, the predicted gap is 1.5 × 73.9 ≈ 111 points. The bivariate slope (79.5) also picks up differences in the other regressors, which these two schools do not have.

exam.concept: Socioeconomic regressors in the API regression (Section 13.1)
exam.stem: Across the 807 schools, the correlation between API and meals (percent of students eligible for free or reduced-price meals) is −0.54. In the multiple regression, the meals coefficient is +0.08 with p ≈ 0.39. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Holding parent education and the other regressors fixed, the data show little evidence of a separate association between meals and API.
options.feedback: Correct. With p ≈ 0.39, the partial effect of meals cannot be distinguished from zero.

options.text: The positive meals coefficient means that reducing student poverty would lower a school's API.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.1 interprets the meals coefficient in the multiple regression.

options.text: Much of the simple negative association between meals and API reflects parent education, which is correlated with meals (r = −0.60).
options.feedback: Correct. Schools with more students on free meals tend to have less-educated parents, and parent education is the dominant predictor.

options.text: The correlation and the coefficient answer different questions, so their signs need not agree.
options.feedback: Correct. The correlation ignores the other regressors; the coefficient holds them fixed.

options.text: The regression shows that student poverty plays no role at all in the API scores of California high schools.
options.feedback: Revisit what an insignificant coefficient does and does not show (Section 13.1).

exam.explanation: Section 13.1: meals is strongly correlated with parent education (r = −0.60). Once edparent and the other regressors are held fixed, meals adds little (+0.08, p ≈ 0.39). The simple correlation of −0.54 mixes meals' own association with that of correlated factors.

exam.stem: In the API data, the percent of fully credentialed teachers (credteach) and the percent with emergency credentials (emerteach) have a correlation of −0.82. Because this correlation is strong but not perfect, OLS can still estimate separate coefficients for both variables in the multiple regression.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Only perfect collinearity prevents OLS from estimating separate coefficients; strong correlation makes them less precise.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit what kind of relationship among regressors prevents OLS from separating their coefficients (Section 13.1).

exam.explanation: Section 13.1: highly correlated regressors make it hard to separate their individual effects and inflate standard errors, but OLS still produces estimates unless one regressor is an exact linear function of the others.

exam.concept: Estimating a production function by OLS (Section 13.2, Key Concept 13.2)
exam.stem: Why does the chapter take natural logarithms of output, capital, and labor before estimating the Cobb-Douglas production function Q = A·K<sup>β₂</sup>·L<sup>β₃</sup> by OLS?

options.text: Logs turn the multiplicative model into one that is linear in its parameters.
options.feedback: Correct. The multiplicative model becomes additive in logs, so OLS can estimate it.

options.text: Logs remove the correlation of the regression errors across the 24 consecutive years of data.
options.feedback: Revisit the reason Section 13.2 gives for the log transformation (Key Concept 13.2).

options.text: Logs turn output, capital, and labor into yearly growth rates, so the regression measures year-to-year changes.
options.feedback: Revisit the reason Section 13.2 gives for the log transformation (Key Concept 13.2).

options.text: Logs force the two elasticities to sum to 1, so constant returns to scale can be imposed.
options.feedback: Revisit the reason Section 13.2 gives for the log transformation (Key Concept 13.2).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.2: ln Q = ln A + β₂ ln K + β₃ ln L is linear in its parameters, so OLS applies; β₁ = ln A, and β₂ and β₃ are output elasticities.

exam.stem: The chapter's estimated Cobb-Douglas function for U.S. manufacturing, 1899–1922, is ln Q = −0.18 + 0.23 ln K + 0.81 ln L. Holding capital fixed, by about how much does predicted output change if labor rises by 10%?

options.text: About 0.81%
options.feedback: Revisit how a coefficient in a log-log model is read (Section 13.2 and Key Concept 13.2).

options.text: About 10.4%
options.feedback: Revisit how a coefficient in a log-log model is read (Section 13.2 and Key Concept 13.2).

options.text: About 8.1%
About 2.3%
options.feedback: Revisit how a coefficient in a log-log model is read (Section 13.2 and Key Concept 13.2).

exam.explanation: Section 13.2: in a log-log model the coefficient is an elasticity, so a 10% rise in labor raises predicted output by about 0.81 × 10 ≈ 8.1%, holding capital fixed.

exam.concept: Testing returns to scale (Section 13.2, Key Concept 13.3)
exam.stem: In the Cobb-Douglas regression, the capital and labor elasticities sum to 1.040. A test of H₀: β₂ + β₃ = 1 gives p = 0.636. What is the best conclusion at the 5% level?

options.text: Returns to scale are increasing, because the estimated sum exceeds 1.
options.feedback: Revisit how Key Concept 13.3 reads the result of this test.

options.text: The data prove that returns to scale are exactly constant.
options.feedback: Revisit what a hypothesis test can and cannot establish (Key Concept 13.3).

options.text: The data are consistent with constant returns to scale: H₀ is not rejected.
options.feedback: Correct. p = 0.636 > 0.05, so the sum of 1.040 is not significantly different from 1.

options.text: Constant returns are rejected, because the estimated sum differs from 1.
options.feedback: Revisit how Key Concept 13.3 reads the result of this test.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.3: the estimated sum 1.040 is close to 1 and p = 0.636 > 0.05, so constant returns are not rejected. Not rejecting is not proof: the data are also consistent with values a little above or below 1.

exam.stem: In the Cobb-Douglas model, constant returns to scale means that doubling capital alone, with labor held fixed, doubles output.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the definition of returns to scale in the chapter's Key Concepts and Section 13.2.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Returns to scale describe scaling all inputs together: under constant returns, doubling both capital and labor doubles output.

exam.explanation: Key Concepts: constant returns to scale means f(λK, λL) = λ·f(K, L); in the Cobb-Douglas form this holds when β₂ + β₃ = 1. Doubling one input alone changes output by the factor 2<sup>β₂</sup> or 2<sup>β₃</sup>.

exam.stem: To plot predicted output in levels from the log Cobb-Douglas regression, the chapter multiplies \( e^{\widehat{\ln Q}} \) by the factor \( e^{s^2/2} \), where \( s \) is the standard error of the regression. Why?

options.text: To convert the estimated elasticities into percentage changes in output
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.2 applies a correction when predicting output levels.

options.text: Because exponentiating the fitted log of output systematically understates the average level of output
options.feedback: Correct. \( e^{\widehat{\ln Q}} \) predicts roughly the median (not the mean) level of output; the factor \( e^{s^2/2} \) corrects this.

options.text: To adjust the predictions for the correlation between ln K and ln L in the annual data
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.2 applies a correction when predicting output levels.

options.text: Because the fitted values of ln Q are measured in base-10 logarithms rather than natural logarithms
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.2 applies a correction when predicting output levels.

exam.explanation: Section 13.2: exponentiating a fitted log gives roughly the median (not the mean) level, so the retransformation correction \( e^{s^2/2} \) is applied. Here \( s \approx 0.058 \), so the factor is only about \( 1.002 \).

exam.stem: For 1949–1969, the chapter's regression of inflation (%) on the unemployment rate (%) has a slope of −1.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: A year with inflation 1 percentage point higher had unemployment about 1.03 points lower, on average.
options.feedback: Revisit how a slope from the chapter's Phillips curve regression is read (Section 13.3).

options.text: Raising unemployment by 1 percentage point would cause inflation to fall by exactly 1.03 points.
options.feedback: Revisit how a slope from the chapter's Phillips curve regression is read (Section 13.3).

options.text: Inflation averaged −1.03% per year over 1949–1969.
options.feedback: Revisit how a slope from the chapter's Phillips curve regression is read (Section 13.3).

options.text: A year with unemployment 1 percentage point higher had inflation about 1.03 points lower, on average.
options.feedback: Correct. The slope compares years that differ by 1 point in the unemployment rate.

exam.explanation: Section 13.3: 1 percentage point more unemployment went with about 1.03 points less inflation in 1949–1969, the classic Phillips trade-off. It is an association, and it did not survive the 1970s.

exam.concept: The Phillips curve after 1970 (Section 13.3, Key Concept 13.4)
exam.stem: For 1970–2014, the bivariate regression of inflation on unemployment has a positive slope with p ≈ 0.42. This establishes that higher unemployment raised inflation after 1970.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what the chapter concludes from the post-1970 bivariate regression, including its p-value (Section 13.3 and Key Concept 13.4).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. With p ≈ 0.42 the positive slope is not statistically significant, and the bivariate model omits expected inflation, so it cannot establish such an effect.

exam.explanation: Section 13.3 and Key Concept 13.4: after 1970 the slope flips sign but is not significant (p ≈ 0.42); the breakdown signals a misspecified bivariate model, not a new causal law.

exam.concept: The omitted variables bias formula (Section 13.3, Key Concept 13.5)
exam.stem: For 1970–2014, the augmented regression of inflation on urate and expected inflation gives β₂ = −0.13 on urate and β₃ = 1.15 on expected inflation, and regressing expected inflation on urate gives γ = 0.34. Using E[b₂] = β₂ + β₃γ, what slope does the formula predict for the bivariate regression of inflation on urate?

options.feedback: Revisit how the omitted variables bias formula combines the three estimates (Section 13.3).
Revisit how the omitted variables bias formula combines the three estimates (Section 13.3).
Revisit how the omitted variables bias formula combines the three estimates (Section 13.3).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.5: the bias β₃γ ≈ 1.15 × 0.34 ≈ +0.39 is positive because expected inflation raises inflation and rose with unemployment after 1970. It turns −0.13 into about +0.26, which matches the chapter's bivariate post-1970 estimate.

exam.concept: Omitted variables bias in the Phillips curve (Section 13.3, Key Concept 13.5)
exam.stem: After 1970, adding expected inflation to the regression of inflation on unemployment turns the unemployment coefficient from positive to −0.13. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Expected inflation helps explain inflation even when unemployment is held fixed.
options.feedback: Correct. Its coefficient in the augmented regression is large and highly significant.

options.text: Omitting expected inflation would bias the unemployment coefficient even if expected inflation were uncorrelated with unemployment.
options.feedback: Revisit the conditions under which the omitted variables bias formula gives a nonzero bias (Section 13.3).

options.text: With many more years of post-1970 data, the bivariate slope would move to about −0.13, because omitted variables bias shrinks as the sample grows.
options.feedback: Revisit whether omitted variables bias depends on sample size (Section 13.3).

options.text: In the bivariate regression, the unemployment coefficient partly picks up the effect of the omitted expected inflation.
options.feedback: Correct. Expected inflation moved with unemployment after 1970, so the bivariate slope absorbs part of its effect.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.5: omitted variables bias needs both β₃ ≠ 0 (expected inflation matters, coefficient ≈ 1.15) and γ ≠ 0 (it moves with unemployment, γ ≈ 0.34); the bivariate slope then absorbs β₃γ. The bias does not shrink with more data; only including the omitted variable removes it.

exam.stem: In the chapter's log-log regression for 26,995 vehicles (1980–2006), the coefficient on ln(curb weight) is −0.56, controlling for ln(horsepower), ln(torque), and model year. Holding the other regressors fixed, how does fuel economy (mpg) differ for a vehicle that is 10% heavier?

options.text: About 5.6% lower
About 5.6 miles per gallon lower
options.feedback: Revisit how coefficients in a log-log model are read, including their units (Section 13.4).

options.text: About 0.56% lower
options.feedback: Revisit how coefficients in a log-log model are read, including their units (Section 13.4).

options.text: About 56% lower
options.feedback: Revisit how coefficients in a log-log model are read, including their units (Section 13.4).

exam.explanation: Section 13.4: in a log-log model the coefficient is an elasticity: 10% more weight goes with about 0.56 × 10 ≈ 5.6% lower mpg, holding horsepower, torque, and year fixed.

exam.concept: The time trend in the fuel-efficiency regression (Section 13.4)
exam.stem: In the same log-log regression, the coefficient on model year is 0.0152. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Holding mpg and weight fixed, horsepower was about 1.5% higher for each later model year.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.4 interprets the year coefficient in the log-log regression.

options.text: Holding the other regressors fixed, fuel economy was about 0.0152 miles per gallon higher for each later model year.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.4 interprets the year coefficient in the log-log regression.

options.text: Holding the other regressors fixed, fuel economy was about 1.5% higher for each later model year.
options.feedback: Correct. With ln(mpg) as the outcome, 0.0152 × 100 ≈ 1.5% per year for vehicles of given power and weight.

options.text: Holding the other regressors fixed, fuel economy was about 1.52 miles per gallon higher for each later model year.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.4 interprets the year coefficient in the log-log regression.

exam.explanation: Section 13.4: with ln(mpg) as the outcome, 0.0152 × 100 ≈ 1.5% per model year, holding horsepower, weight, and torque fixed. It measures technical progress for a vehicle of given size and power, not the change in average mpg.

exam.stem: The fuel-efficiency regression uses standard errors clustered by manufacturer (39 manufacturers, about 690 vehicles each). Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Clustering is needed because the dependent variable, ln(mpg), is measured in logs.
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.4 clusters the standard errors (Key Concept 13.6).

options.text: Vehicles from the same manufacturer share technology and design, so their errors are likely correlated.
options.feedback: Correct. Shared platforms and engineering teams make errors within a manufacturer move together.

options.text: With 26,995 vehicles, clustering is unnecessary because a large sample removes the correlation within manufacturers.
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.4 clusters the standard errors despite the large sample.

options.text: Clustering by manufacturer estimates a separate weight elasticity for each manufacturer.
options.feedback: Revisit what clustering changes in the regression output (Key Concept 13.6).

options.text: Default standard errors that ignore this grouping would tend to understate the uncertainty in the estimates.
options.feedback: Correct. Correlated errors carry less independent information than 26,995 separate draws.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.6: cluster-robust standard errors allow errors to be correlated within each manufacturer. They leave the coefficients unchanged; ignoring the clustering would understate uncertainty. In these data the clustered standard error of the weight elasticity is about nine times the default one.

exam.stem: From 1985 to 2006, average fuel economy of the vehicles in the data stayed near 25 mpg while their average weight and horsepower rose. Together with the positive year coefficient, this suggests that technology gains were largely offset by heavier, more powerful vehicles.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Holding weight and power fixed, mpg improved over time, but heavier and more powerful vehicles, which get lower mpg, used up those gains.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's discussion of why average fuel economy stagnated (Section 13.4).

exam.explanation: Section 13.4 (the weight paradox): technical progress raised mpg for a vehicle of given weight and power, but average weight rose from about 3,100 to 3,900 pounds and horsepower roughly doubled between 1985 and 2006, so average mpg stayed near 25.

exam.concept: Comparing insurance plans without random assignment (Section 13.5, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: Suppose researchers compared the medical spending of people who chose generous insurance with that of people who chose plans with high cost-sharing, without random assignment. Why might the spending difference not measure the effect of insurance?

options.text: Because spending would have to be clustered by family before the two group means could be compared
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.5 relies on random assignment to compare insurance plans.

options.text: Because people who choose generous plans tend to differ in health or income, which also affects spending
options.feedback: Correct. Self-selection mixes the plan's effect with the traits of the people who choose it.

options.text: Because plan indicators usually explain little of the variation in spending, which makes their coefficients unreliable
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.5 relies on random assignment to compare insurance plans.

options.text: Because comparing average spending across plans requires the plan indicators to be uncorrelated with one another
options.feedback: Revisit why Section 13.5 relies on random assignment to compare insurance plans.

exam.explanation: Key Concepts and Section 13.5: when people self-select into plans, traits such as health or income affect both the plan chosen and spending, so the comparison mixes the plan's effect with selection. Random assignment closes this channel.

exam.stem: In the RAND experiment's first year (5,639 observations), the regression of medical spending on plan indicators, with free care as the omitted category, gives an intercept of $2,154 and a coefficient of −$1,108 on the 95% coinsurance plan. What is the predicted average spending for people in the 95% plan?

options.feedback: Revisit how an indicator coefficient relates to the omitted category (Section 13.5).
Revisit how an indicator coefficient relates to the omitted category (Section 13.5).
Revisit how an indicator coefficient relates to the omitted category (Section 13.5).

exam.explanation: Section 13.5: with free care as the base, the intercept ($2,154) is the free-care mean and each plan coefficient is the difference from it: 2,154 − 1,108 = $1,046, the 95% plan's mean.

exam.concept: What random assignment does (Section 13.5, Key Concept 13.7)
exam.stem: Because the RAND experiment assigned plans at random, the free-care group and the 95% coinsurance group have the same average age in the sample.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what random assignment ensures about the groups, and in what sense (Key Concept 13.7).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Randomization makes the groups comparable in expectation; in any one sample, averages differ somewhat by chance.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.7: random assignment removes systematic differences in observed and unobserved traits, but chance differences remain in any one sample; standard errors account for them.

exam.stem: Relative to free care (mean spending $2,154), the RAND first-year coefficients are −$757 for the 25% coinsurance plan (p < 0.001), −$368 for the 50% plan (p ≈ 0.55), and −$1,108 for the 95% plan (p < 0.001); a joint F-test that all plan coefficients are zero gives p < 0.001. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The plans jointly matter: the hypothesis that all plan coefficients are zero is rejected at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Correct. The joint F-test's p < 0.001 rejects H₀.

options.text: The 50% plan's estimate is too imprecise to distinguish its spending from that under free care.
options.feedback: Correct. With p ≈ 0.55, the data are consistent with no difference from free care.

options.text: The estimated coefficients become steadily more negative as the coinsurance rate rises from 25% to 50% to 95%.
options.feedback: Revisit the three coinsurance coefficients reported in the stem (Section 13.5).

options.text: The 25% plan's coefficient means that 25% coinsurance cuts spending by about 25% relative to free care.
options.feedback: Revisit how the plan coefficients are measured and what they are compared with (Section 13.5).

options.text: Because plans were randomly assigned, the coefficients estimate causal effects of plan generosity on spending.
options.feedback: Correct. Random assignment removes selection, so differences in mean spending are causal.

exam.explanation: Section 13.5: the joint test rejects (F = 11.39); the 25% and 95% plans spend significantly less than free care, but the 50% estimate is imprecise. −$757 is about 35% of the $2,154 free-care mean, and the 50% estimate (−$368) lies between zero and the 25% estimate, so spending does not fall steadily with the coinsurance rate.

exam.stem: In the South African study, mean weight-for-age z-scores (waz) were −0.414 in 1993 and −0.069 in 1998 in low-treatment communities, and −0.545 in 1993 and 0.321 in 1998 in high-treatment communities. What is the difference-in-differences estimate of the effect of clinic access?

options.feedback: Revisit the difference-in-differences formula in Section 13.6.
Revisit the difference-in-differences formula in Section 13.6.
Revisit the difference-in-differences formula in Section 13.6.

exam.explanation: Section 13.6: DiD = change in the treated group − change in the control group = 0.866 − 0.345 ≈ 0.52 standard deviations, matching the regression's interaction coefficient.

exam.concept: The identifying assumption of DiD (Section 13.6, Key Concept 13.8)
exam.stem: The DiD estimate credits clinic access with the extra improvement in high-treatment communities only if, without the new clinics, their average waz would have changed by the same amount as in low-treatment communities.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. That is the parallel trends assumption: the control group's change stands in for the treated group's counterfactual change.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the key assumption behind difference-in-differences (Key Concept 13.8).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.8: DiD is unbiased only under parallel trends, so the low-treatment communities' change must show how the high-treatment communities would have evolved without the clinics.

exam.stem: The chapter estimates waz = β₁ + β₂ hightreat + β₃ post + β₄ postXhigh + u, where hightreat = 1 for high-treatment communities, post = 1 for 1998, and postXhigh is their product. What does β₂ measure?

options.text: The average difference in waz between high- and low-treatment communities in 1993
options.feedback: Correct. With post = 0, the two groups' predictions differ by β₂.

options.text: The effect of clinic access on waz in high-treatment communities
options.feedback: Revisit how each coefficient of the DiD regression maps to a cell of the table of group means (Section 13.6).

options.text: The change in average waz from 1993 to 1998 in low-treatment communities
options.feedback: Revisit how each coefficient of the DiD regression maps to a cell of the table of group means (Section 13.6).

options.text: The average waz of the children living in low-treatment communities in the 1993 survey
options.feedback: Revisit how each coefficient of the DiD regression maps to a cell of the table of group means (Section 13.6).

exam.explanation: Section 13.6: β₁ is the low-treatment mean in 1993, β₂ the 1993 gap between high- and low-treatment communities, β₃ the low-treatment change, and β₄ the DiD effect. Here β₂ ≈ −0.13 (p ≈ 0.51).

exam.concept: Validity and inference in the DiD study (Section 13.6)
exam.stem: Which statements about the chapter's South African clinic study (1,071 children in 54 communities) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Standard errors are clustered by community because children in one community share conditions that correlate their outcomes.
options.feedback: Correct. That within-community correlation is why the chapter clusters by community.

options.text: Group differences that stay constant over time do not bias the DiD estimate.
options.feedback: Correct. Each group's own before/after change removes its time-invariant features.

options.text: Because the DiD estimate is significant at the 5% level, the data confirm the parallel trends assumption.
options.feedback: Revisit what a significance test of the DiD coefficient can and cannot establish (Section 13.6).

options.text: Because clinic access was assigned to communities, not children, the study's treatment varies at the community level.
options.feedback: Correct. Treatment is a community-level variable, which is why the analysis treats communities as the clusters.

exam.explanation: Section 13.6 and Key Concept 13.8: DiD removes time-invariant differences between groups, but parallel trends is an assumption that a significant DiD coefficient cannot confirm. Treatment varies at the community level, so standard errors are clustered by community, which reduces statistical power.

exam.concept: Interpreting the regression discontinuity estimate (Section 13.7, Key Concept 13.9)
exam.stem: In the regression vote = β₁ + β₂ win + β₃ margin for 1,297 U.S. Senate elections (1914–2010), where vote is the party's vote share in the next election, margin is its vote margin in the current election (negative after a loss), and win = 1 if margin > 0, the coefficient on win is 4.8. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Every incumbent senator receives exactly 4.8 more percentage points than a challenger would in the next election.
options.feedback: Revisit what the coefficient on win measures in an RD regression (Section 13.7, Key Concept 13.9).

options.text: Each extra point of winning margin in the current election raises next-election vote share by 4.8 percentage points.
options.feedback: Revisit what the coefficient on win measures in an RD regression (Section 13.7, Key Concept 13.9).

options.text: Near the threshold, barely winning rather than barely losing raises next-election vote share by about 4.8 percentage points.
options.feedback: Correct. The coefficient on win is the jump in next-election vote share at margin = 0.

options.text: Near the threshold, barely winning raises the vote share in the current election by about 4.8 percentage points.
options.feedback: Revisit what the coefficient on win measures in an RD regression (Section 13.7, Key Concept 13.9).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.9: β₂ is the jump in next-election vote share at margin = 0: barely winning rather than barely losing raises it by about 4.8 percentage points (95% CI about 3.1 to 6.5). It is a local effect for close elections.

exam.stem: In the 1,297 Senate elections, next-election vote share averages about 21.7 percentage points higher after a win than after a loss. This simple comparison is a better estimate of the incumbency advantage than the RD estimate because it uses every election, not only close ones.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit why the chapter compares candidates who barely won with those who barely lost (Section 13.7).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Landslide winners are much stronger than landslide losers, so the simple gap mixes candidate strength with incumbency; RD compares near-identical candidates at the threshold.

exam.explanation: Section 13.7: comparing all winners with all losers suffers from selection bias, since winners are stronger candidates. RD isolates the effect of incumbency where winning is as good as random.

exam.concept: Assumptions and features of the RD design (Section 13.7)
exam.stem: Which statements about the chapter's regression discontinuity design for Senate elections are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It requires candidates to be randomly assigned to parties before each election.
options.feedback: Revisit what creates quasi-random assignment in an RD design (Section 13.7).

options.text: It assumes candidates cannot precisely control whether they land just above or just below the threshold.
options.feedback: Correct. The chapter's design assumes no manipulation of the vote margin.

options.text: Including margin as a regressor separates the jump at margin = 0 from the smooth relationship between margin and next-election vote share.
options.feedback: Correct. Without it, the win coefficient would also pick up the general tendency of bigger winners to do better next time.

options.text: It is credible only if the regression also controls for candidate quality, fundraising, and media coverage.
options.feedback: Revisit why units near the threshold can be compared directly (Section 13.7).

exam.explanation: Section 13.7 and Key Concept 13.9: near the threshold, winning is as good as random, provided margins cannot be manipulated. Controlling for margin captures the smooth trend, so no other controls are needed for identification.

exam.stem: The 2SLS estimate for 64 former colonies is log GDP per capita = 1.91 + 0.944 × avexpr, where avexpr measures protection against expropriation (0–10). By about what percentage is GDP per capita predicted to be higher for a country whose avexpr is 1 point higher?

options.text: About 94%
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.8 converts the coefficient into a change in the GDP level.

options.text: About 157%
options.feedback: Correct: e<sup>0.944</sup> ≈ 2.57, so GDP per capita is about 2.57 times as high, a 157% increase.

options.text: About 257%
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.8 converts the coefficient into a change in the GDP level.

options.text: About 61%
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 13.8 converts the coefficient into a change in the GDP level.

exam.explanation: Section 13.8: a 1-unit change in x multiplies y by e<sup>b</sup> when y is in logs. With b = 0.944 that factor is about 2.57, so GDP per capita is about 157% higher; the approximation 100 × b (94%) is poor for a coefficient this large.

exam.concept: Conditions for a valid instrument (Section 13.8, Key Concept 13.10)
exam.stem: The chapter uses log settler mortality (logem4) as an instrument for institutions (avexpr) in a regression of log GDP per capita on avexpr. Which pair of conditions must logem4 satisfy?

options.text: It must be correlated with avexpr and also have its own direct effect on log GDP per capita.
options.feedback: Revisit the two conditions an instrument must meet (Key Concept 13.10).

options.text: It must be correlated with avexpr and affect log GDP per capita only through avexpr.
options.feedback: Correct. These are relevance and exogeneity (the exclusion restriction).

options.text: It must be uncorrelated with both avexpr and log GDP per capita.
options.feedback: Revisit the two conditions an instrument must meet (Key Concept 13.10).

options.text: It must be strongly correlated with log GDP per capita and uncorrelated with avexpr.
options.feedback: Revisit the two conditions an instrument must meet (Key Concept 13.10).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 13.10: a valid instrument is relevant (correlated with the endogenous regressor) and exogenous (no direct effect on the outcome, so uncorrelated with the error).

exam.stem: In the first-stage regression of avexpr on logem4, the F-statistic for the instrument is 16.3. What does this tell us?

options.text: The OLS estimate of the effect of institutions on log GDP per capita is unbiased.
options.feedback: Revisit what the first-stage regression can and cannot tell us (Section 13.8).

options.text: The first stage confirms that settler mortality is uncorrelated with the error in the GDP regression.
options.feedback: Revisit what the first-stage regression can and cannot tell us (Section 13.8).

options.text: Settler mortality explains most of the variation in institutions across the 64 colonies.
options.feedback: Revisit what the first-stage F-statistic measures (Section 13.8).

options.text: The instrument is strong enough by the chapter's rule of thumb.
options.feedback: Correct. F = 16.3 exceeds the rule-of-thumb threshold of 10.

exam.explanation: Section 13.8: F = 16.3 > 10, so the instrument is not weak, even though settler mortality explains only about 27% of the variation in institutions. The first stage checks relevance only; exogeneity cannot be tested this way and rests on the historical argument.

exam.stem: For the 64 former colonies, the 2SLS estimate of the effect of avexpr on log GDP per capita is about 80% larger than the OLS estimate. Which explanation does the chapter give?

options.text: Measurement error in avexpr biases OLS toward zero.
options.feedback: Correct. Attenuation from measurement error is the chapter's explanation for the smaller OLS estimate.

options.text: Reverse causation from income to institutions biases OLS toward zero.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's discussion of the sources of bias in OLS and their directions (Section 13.8).

options.text: Omitted factors such as culture and geography bias OLS toward zero.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's discussion of the sources of bias in OLS and their directions (Section 13.8).

options.text: IV estimates are always larger than OLS estimates, whatever the source of bias.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's discussion of the sources of bias in OLS and their directions (Section 13.8).

exam.explanation: Section 13.8: omitted variables and reverse causation would, if anything, bias OLS upward. Since the IV estimate (0.94) exceeds OLS (0.52), the chapter attributes the gap to attenuation bias from measurement error in the institutions measure.

exam.stem: A researcher receives data in three files and finds negative ages, missing incomes, and gender coded as 'M', 'm', and 'Female'. Which workflow follows the chapter's best practices?

options.text: Correct the errors by hand in the original files, so that every later user starts from clean data.
options.feedback: Revisit the best practices listed in Section 13.9.

options.text: Delete every variable that has missing values or inconsistent codes before running any regressions.
options.feedback: Revisit the best practices listed in Section 13.9.

options.text: Keep the raw files unchanged, make every correction in a script, and report what was changed or dropped.
options.feedback: Correct. This preserves the raw data, makes the cleaning reproducible, and keeps it transparent.

options.text: Replace each problem value with the sample mean, so that no observations or variables are ever lost.
options.feedback: Revisit the best practices listed in Section 13.9.

exam.explanation: Section 13.9: document everything, preserve raw data, use scripts rather than manual edits, validate before and after cleaning, and report how many observations were dropped and why.

exam.stem: Suppose a researcher regresses U.S. quarterly GDP growth on interest rates for 1990–2019 and expects the errors in nearby quarters to be correlated. Which standard errors does the chapter recommend?

options.text: HAC (Newey–West) standard errors
options.feedback: Correct. HAC standard errors allow for heteroskedasticity and correlation across nearby periods.

options.text: Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's guide to choosing standard errors (Key Takeaways, Sections 13.2 and 13.4).

options.text: Standard errors clustered by quarter
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's guide to choosing standard errors (Key Takeaways, Sections 13.2 and 13.4).

options.text: Default standard errors, since 120 quarters is a large sample
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's guide to choosing standard errors (Key Takeaways, Sections 13.2 and 13.4).

exam.explanation: Key Takeaways: HC1 for cross-sections, cluster-robust for grouped data, and HAC for time series with serially correlated errors, as in the Cobb-Douglas and Phillips curve regressions.

exam.stem: Suppose researchers want the effect of serving in the military on later earnings. Men who volunteer differ from those who do not, but a lottery randomly decided who was eligible for the draft, and eligible men were much more likely to serve. The researchers use eligibility as a source of variation in who served. Which method fits this setting best?

options.text: Randomized control trial
options.feedback: Revisit what kind of variation each causal method exploits (Sections 13.5–13.8).

options.text: Regression discontinuity
options.feedback: Revisit what kind of variation each causal method exploits (Sections 13.5–13.8).

options.text: Instrumental variables
options.feedback: Correct. Eligibility shifts service but is randomly assigned, so it can serve as an instrument for the endogenous choice to serve.

options.text: Difference-in-differences
options.feedback: Revisit what kind of variation each causal method exploits (Sections 13.5–13.8).

exam.explanation: Sections 13.5–13.8: service itself was chosen (endogenous), but draft eligibility was assigned by lottery and strongly shifted service. A randomly assigned variable that moves the endogenous regressor and affects earnings only through it is an instrument, so IV/2SLS fits.
